10319-dave-darrin-s-third-year-at-annapo:
H. Irving Hancock published this naval school story in 1911, following Dave Darrin into his third year at Annapolis. Dave now leads second-class midshipmen, a post that tests both his skill and his temper. The book is one of a series meant to praise Navy discipline and boyish honor.

Rivals, a trouble-making fop, football, a class meeting that sits as jury, and a disputed charge keep Dave busy. He must prove his training, calm his friends, and face blame with fairness. Readers get a brisk, patriotic tale of cadet life, sport, and leadership at sea school.
10677-biographical-memorials-of-james-og:
Thaddeus Mason Harris, a Boston scholar, published Biographical Memorials of James Oglethorpe in 1841, dedicated to the Georgia Historical Society. Oglethorpe founded the colony of Georgia in North America, and Harris gathers the record of his life, service, and plans for the new settlement. Savannah friends helped bring the work to print.

The memorials trace Oglethorpe from soldier and reformer to colonial founder, with attention to his aims for debtors and settlers. Harris writes with respect for his subject and care for documents. Readers interested in Georgia's origins get an early, earnest life of the colony's founder.
11104-in-morocco:
Edith Wharton published this 1920 travel book on Morocco, dedicated to General Lyautey, France's Resident General, and Madame Lyautey, whose kindness made a long-dreamed journey surpass dreaming. Wharton travelled in 1918, when German submarines made the sea trip from Marseilles to Casablanca slow, so she crossed country by military motor, with only one month before the November rains.

Chapters cover Rabat and Salé, Volubilis, Moulay Idriss and Meknez, Fez, Marrakech, harems and ceremonies, Lyautey's work, a sketch of Moroccan history, and Moroccan architecture. At Marrakech, Wharton visits the Menara, a Sultan's pleasure-house above a reservoir, where the Chief of the Guild of Wool-Merchants takes tea in the loggia. The book captures Morocco at a moment of transition, just before it opened to mass travel.
11297-travels-through-the-empire-of-moro:
John Buffa, a physician to the British forces, published his Travels Through the Empire of Morocco in London in 1810, with a map. Buffa reached Morocco after a frustrated posting to Gibraltar, where he waited months for a commission that never came. then crossed at the request of the British consul general at Tangier to attend patients in Barbary. His narrative describes Moroccan towns, government, customs, and medicine as a newcomer saw them.

The book's interest lies in its practical eye: Buffa writes as a doctor and observer, not a romantic traveler. Court intrigue, quarantine duties, and daily life all appear. For historians of North Africa, it offers an early British account written before French colonization reshaped the region.
11510-fascinating-san-francisco:
This 1924 booklet, Fascinating San Francisco, opens with Bret Harte's warder of two continents and a train of admirers from Dana to Stevenson, Harte to Mencken. Kipling's drypoint, San Francisco has only one drawback, it is hard to leave, sets the tone. The city, cradled as a drowsy Spanish pueblo, reared as a child of the mines, and fed on gold-spangled Argonaut days. appears as a dashing western beauty with exotic ancestry, intensely American yet cosmopolitan, with alien tongues on its streets.

Inez Haynes Irwin warns strangers to see California before entering San Francisco, lest they never leave. The booklet aims to keep the curtain up, guiding readers through the bay peninsula. For city enthusiasts, it captures San Francisco between earthquake rebuilding and modern growth.
13150-through-the-grand-canyon-from-wyom:
E. L. Kolb's Through the Grand Canyon from Wyoming to Mexico, in a new edition of 1915 with a foreword by Owen Wister, records a river journey by boat. Kolb and his brother took photographs along the way, and seventy-two plates illustrate the text. The journey starts in Wyoming and runs the Colorado through the canyon toward Mexico.

Kolb describes ranches with poplar avenues and alfalfa fields, a post office with mail from home, and saddle horses for a ride to Vernal. At day's end he watches haze turn temples and spires from heliotrope to lavender to deep purple, until twilight fills the canyon. The book is both adventure and picture record, and it helped fix the canyon in the public mind.
13286-the-story-of-crisco:
The Story of Crisco, eleventh edition, 1913 to 1916, from the Procter and Gamble Company of Cincinnati, is a cookbook built around the new shortening. Contents run from things to remember and hints to young cooks to soups, fish, meats, vegetables, salads, puddings, pastries, breads, cakes, and a calendar of dinners. The book costs twenty-five cents and teaches thrift and method.

It advises using dinner leftovers in salads, with thinly sliced cold potatoes, green peas, and string beans as especially good choices, and chicken, lobster, and salmon salads as the most widely known. A February dinner gives Bombay toast, boiled halibut with lobster sauce, roast capon, and beet and potato salad. The book is a classic of early twentieth-century American home cooking.
13746-gold-sport-and-coffee-planting-in-:
Robert H. Elliot spent thirty-eight years as a planter in Mysore, India, and wrote this 1898 account. He covers gold mining, sport, coffee planting in Mysore and Coorg, and Mysore government. Chapters also treat the Representative Assembly, the Indian Congress, caste, and the silver question. A coloured map fronts the volume.

Elliot describes scenery, waterfalls, hunting, and plantation work in full detail. He dedicates the book to Sir K. Sheshadri Iyer, Dewan of Mysore. His views reflect a British planter's outlook, with praise for local rulers and frank talk of trade. The book serves as a source for colonial agriculture and politics. It also reads as a memoir of a long Indian career.
14866-animal-sanctuaries-in-labrador-an-:
Lieutenant Colonel William Wood addresses the second annual meeting of Canada's Commission of Conservation at Quebec in January 1911, pleading for animal sanctuaries in Labrador. Published at Ottawa, the address appeals to all for whom wild nature is a glory of the earth and an heirloom for posterity.

Wood asks help to keep Labrador's animal life from being wantonly done to death, and argues that the three classes most interested in wild life need not disagree. Business, sport and science can share a common cause. Short and urgent, the address is an early Canadian conservation text, calling for protected ground before hunting and trade empty a wilderness.
15409-an-elegy-wrote-in-a-country-church:
Thomas Gray's Elegy Wrote in a Country Church Yard, first published in 1751, appears here with the Eton College manuscript, in a 1951 reprint from the Augustan Reprint Society. George Sherburn of Harvard wrote the introduction, and the first edition text comes from a copy in the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles.

The Elegy itself is Gray's famous meditation in a country churchyard, on humble lives, unmarked graves, and fame that never came. Printing it beside the Eton manuscript lets readers compare draft and finished poem, line by line. For students of English poetry, the slim volume is a working tool: a great short poem in a clean text, with its early form close at hand for study.
165-mcteague-a-story-of-san-francisco:
McTeague, a huge and slow dentist on Polk Street, lives for food, beer, and his pipe. Frank Norris's McTeague follows him from a quiet practice to marriage, greed, and murder. His friend Marcus courts Trina, then steps aside, and McTeague marries her instead.

Trina wins a lottery prize and hoards it while McTeague loses his license and his temper. Jealousy, drink, and the gold fever of the Sierras pull the pair apart. Norris tracks appetite and fate with naturalist force. The novel ends in the desert, a landmark of American realism.
16526-morocco:
S. L. Bensusan describes Morocco and A. S. Forrest paints it in this 1904 travel volume from Adam and Charles Black. The route runs from Cape Spartel and Tangier to Djedida, along the Moorish road to the gates of Marrakesh, and through a southern province to the argan forest. A slave market, green tea, and local politics all get chapters.

Bensusan writes with a traveler's eye for color, custom, and street life, while Forrest's pictures add the visual record. The book captures Morocco just before modern change, when old cities and desert roads still ruled. Readers of classic travel writing will find it rich, lively, and full of place.
16711-life-and-labors-of-elder-john-klin:
Benjamin Funk drew this 1900 life of Elder John Kline, martyr missionary, from Kline's own diary, issued by the Brethren house at Elgin, Illinois. It opens at his grave in the Linville's Creek German Baptist churchyard in Rockingham County, Virginia, where a marble slab bears his name. Funk muses on death, on the butterfly's wing, and on great endings as great beginnings.

Funk follows Kline's work as a Brethren preacher, his travels, and his death as a martyr, in diary form. The tone is devout and plain, with a strong sense of a life given to faith. Readers of church history and Brethren life will find a warm, first-hand life story, told by a man who knew the ground Kline walked.
17008-a-counter-blaste-to-tobacco:
King James I wrote this short blast against tobacco in 1604, and Edmund Goldsmid edited this 1884 reprint from the London text. The king scolds a new national habit as foul, costly, and vain, and he warns that peace and wealth have bred soft delights in his people. His address to dear countrymen sets the tone: plain, royal, and tart.

Short as it is, the piece shows an early modern ruler using print to fight a fashion he saw as a public harm. Its old spelling and sharp jokes make it fun to read aloud. Smokers, historians, and fans of royal prose will enjoy a king's grumble that still sounds oddly current four centuries on.
17469-berry-and-co:
Dornford Yates wrote this comic novel for Ward, Lock and Company in London and Melbourne, following his earlier Berry books such as Jonah and Co. and The Brother of Daphne. The chapters read like linked episodes. Each is headed by teasing summaries: how Will Noggin was fooled, how Daphne wrote for help, and how Nobby came to sleep upon the narrator's bed.

Berry, Daphne, Jill, and their circle move through scrapes with thieves, outbidding, lamps in hand, and husbands given the slip, all told in Yates's light, witty voice. Readers get an upper-class English comedy of manners and mishaps, where talk and timing carry the fun. It remains a pleasant example of interwar light fiction.
18443-parrot-co:
Harold MacGrath wrote this novel, published by A. L. Burt in New York in 1913, with four color illustrations by André Castaigne. Its chapters carry names like East Is East, A Man with a Past, Two Days of Paradise, and The Game of Gossip, moving from mystery to open conflict.

The story turns on a man with a past, two brothers, and a woman's reason, with letters, cables, and a battle among its later chapters. MacGrath, known for The Best Man and The Carpet from Bagdad, writes a tale of secrets, loyalty, and reunion, where old ties return after ten years apart.
19223-at-war-with-pontiac-or-the-totem-o:
Kirk Munroe wrote this 1922 boys' tale, At War with Pontiac, or The Totem of the Bear, with pictures by J. Finnemore. It follows redcoats and redskins on the frontier after the French wars, as Pontiac declares war and Major Hester is taken prisoner. Donald sets forth on a perilous mission and is saved from a terrible death.

Major Hester refuses to give up a prisoner to Mahng for torture, since the man's child saved his life, and bids sachems lay grievances before Sir William Johnson. Threats of owl-haunted houses follow. Young readers get a stirring frontier tale of war, honour, and the tangled loyalties of the pays d'en haut.
19398-by-right-of-conquest-or-with-corte:
G. A. Henty wrote this boys' tale, By Right of Conquest, or With Cortez in Mexico. Chapters run from a startling proposal and a voyage to shipwreck, Anahuac, Tezcuco, palace life, Cortez, the massacre of Cholula, Mexico, a treasure room, insurrection, and the passage of the causeway. The hero joins Cortez's march.

A young Englishman, bound to unknown parts, learns Aztec splendour and Spanish conquest from inside, facing gods, victims, and war. Henty's tale favours the conquerors, as was common in its day. Young readers get a stirring, if dated, adventure of Mexico's conquest.
20041-men-s-sewed-straw-hats-report-of-t:
Under section 315 of the Tariff Act of 1922, the Tariff Commission studied men's sewed straw hats. Its report went to the President of the United States. The study weighed costs of making the hats at home and abroad. One member, Commissioner Costigan, agreed in part and dissented in part.

Inside are cost figures, trade facts, and the split view of the panel. Such reports helped set duties on imported goods in the 1920s. Readers who study trade policy can see how the law worked in one small trade. A straw hat becomes a test case for tariffs.
20259-frontier-boys-in-frisco:
Capt. Wyn Roosevelt published Frontier Boys in Frisco in 1911, a boys' adventure tale. Jim Darlington tells Bob Ketchel he would love a plan at once. Bob, he says, can drive a locomotive as well as any team. Back in Kansas, Bob drove a four-horse team across the plains.

Nothing beats the real horse, Bob replies, but he can manage this fire eater. Steam, speed, and San Francisco give the frontier boys a new stage. The series moves its heroes from plains to city and rail. Readers get fast, friendly adventure in the classic boys' series mold.
20407-notes-and-queries-number-184-may-7:
Number 184 of Notes and Queries appeared on May 7, 1853. Readers used the journal to trade questions and answers on books, history, and old customs. Every issue mixes short notes from scholars, clergy, and keen amateurs.

One writer reports a curious printed fragment that had lately come into his hands. He thinks it worth notice on several counts, above all for lovers of early ballad poetry. The fragment seems to come from an unknown edition of an old work. Such finds were the journal's lifeblood: small pieces of the past, printed so others could help place them.
21365-rob-harlow-s-adventures-a-story-of:
Teenager Rob Harlow joins a small private naturalist expedition up a Paraguay river into the Grand Chaco in George Manville Fenn's South American tale. Their Italian captain waits with the big vessel while the party rows upriver. His son Giovanni begs to come, and against the adults' doubts he is allowed.

Serpents, jaguars, pumas, insects, and attacks by local peoples follow, with men lost and found again half out of their minds. Even the two boys quarrel over a silly misunderstanding. Fenn treats the Chaco as he treated Africa and Burma: a green, dangerous classroom where natural history and survival arrive together, page by page.
21561-fra-angelico:
J. B. Supino's Fra Angelico, in Leader Scott's English version of 1902, praises a painter of pure celestial forms. Among all masters, Supino says, Fra Angelico alone made the human shape carry a divine spirit with such simple line. His Annunciation at San Marco fronts the book.

Chapters trace the friar-painter at Cortona and Perugia, then Fiesole, Florence, Rome, and Orvieto. Tradition shows him praying before he dared to paint the Virgin. Lists of pictures and an index of plates back the text. The book suits lovers of early Italian art who want life and works told together.
21987-the-village-pulpit-volume-ii-trini:
Village preachers get a full season of sermons in S. Baring-Gould's The Village Pulpit, volume two, running from Trinity to Advent in its second edition of 1886. Sixty-six short sermons or full outlines cover each Sunday and chief holy days of the Christian year. Sermon thirty-seven opens with Christian unity on Trinity Sunday. Great surprises, the Holy Communion, and rash decisions follow week by week.

Baring-Gould was a prolific parson and novelist, and his outlines are built for working clergy: a text, a theme, and a clear path through it. The measure of sin and casting blame show his moral directness. The two volumes together formed a complete course for a year of Sundays. It is a practical relic of Victorian parish life.
22510-documentary-history-of-the-rio-gra:
Adolph F. Bandelier compiled a documentary history of the Rio Grande Pueblos of New Mexico. Part one gives a bibliographic introduction to the sources. Bandelier was a pioneering scholar of the Southwest's peoples.

The region's geography, he says, is too well known to need mention. Folklore and tradition, though, carry decisive importance in many cases. He touches them only when the sources themselves allude to them. That discipline marks the work as documentary, not legendary. Bandelier lets Spanish records speak for the Pueblo past. Readers get the paper trail of missions, pueblos, and colonial rule. It remains a foundation work for historians of the Rio Grande valley.
22542-jesus-the-christ-a-study-of-the-me:
James E. Talmage wrote Jesus the Christ, a study of the Messiah and His mission. It follows ancient and modern scripture, per its subtitle. Talmage wrote it for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

He entered the work under appointment from presiding church authorities. The completed book was read to the First Presidency for approval. The Council of the Twelve also reviewed and approved it. Yet it presents, he stresses, his personal belief and conviction. Talmage traces Christ's life from premortal existence to resurrection. Each event is weighed against scripture, history, and doctrine in detail. The book became a standard Latter-day Saint reference. Readers get systematic theology joined to a life of Christ.
22607-the-book-hunter-in-london-historic:
The Book-Hunter in London is a study of London's book trade and its collectors, with portraits and illustrations. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. The author ranges through bookshops, stalls, and sale rooms, gathering history and anecdote along the way.

In the closing words, the author thanks a crowd of friends and booksellers who shared advice and information. Almost everyone proved courteous; the geniality of book collectors, the author jokes, is proverbial, though a rare churlish specimen does turn up. Such warmth fills the book's sketches of dealers and hunters. It remains a rich source for the social history of bookselling in the world's great book city.
23193-the-white-chief-a-legend-of-northe:
The White Chief is billed as a legend of northern Mexico. Its opening surveys the land through a telescope. To the west, the view changes: far off lie tilled fields in a narrow band along a bright river.

Those fields mark the settlements of New Mexico, an oasis watered by the Rio del Norte. The tale is careful to say that its own scene does not lie there. That refusal sets the stage for wilder ground beyond the settled strip. Readers get a frontier legend framed by contrast between farmed river land and the open country beyond.
2356-tommy-and-co:
Jerome K. Jerome's Tommy and Co. follows a group of young Londoners making their way in the world of journalism, art, and love. The novel's heroine Tommy, a spirited girl in a man's world, anchors a set of comic romances and professional scrapes. Jerome's humor is gentler here than in his famous travel books, but just as observant.

The book captures Edwardian London's bohemian edges: studios, newspaper offices, and cheap lodgings. Its characters muddle toward happiness with charm. Readers of light Edwardian fiction will enjoy its warmth. Jerome's heroine Tommy was unusual for her time: a working girl with ambition.
23648-gaspar-the-gaucho-a-story-of-the-g:
Captain Mayne Reid, inventor of the Wild West tale, set this adventure in the Gran Chaco of South America. It is the vast plain between the Salado and Parana rivers, running up toward Paraguay and the Brazilian frontier. His hero is Gaspar the Gaucho, a plainsman whose band of friends undertakes a voyage across country that few outsiders knew.

Time and again the party falls into danger — lost horses, hostile country, narrow escapes. Each time, their bush-craft, learned by Reid himself in the American-Mexican War, carries them through. It is a vintage Victorian adventure: brisk, outdoor, and fond of the gaucho's skill with horse, rope, and open ground.
24296-six-days-of-the-irish-republic-a-n:
L. G. Redmond-Howard, nephew and biographer of the Irish leader John Redmond, wrote this narrative and critical account of the latest phase of Irish politics. It was published in London and Dublin in 1916 and passed by the censor. It tells of six days of the Irish Republic, opening on Easter Monday 1916. Dubliners saw armed, organized men capture every strategic point in the capital within a single hour and hold it in the name of a new Republic.

Chapters run from A Bolt from the Blue and Just Before the Battle through Battle, Surrender and Collapse, and Aftermath. Later chapters cover Sinn Fein and German Gold, Minds and Men, Remoter Causes of the Rebellion, and Reflections Towards Reconstruction. Redmond-Howard dedicates the book to Wilfred Meynell, one of the few honest Englishmen ashamed of English rule in Ireland. Readers get a first-hand history of the Rising.
24450-bones-being-further-adventures-in-:
Edgar Wallace published this collection in London and Melbourne as further adventures in Commissioner Sanders' country. It follows his earlier Sanders of the River. Sanders, a colonial commissioner in West Africa, rules a river district where official reports hide far more than they tell. His young officer Hamilton, nicknamed Bones, blunders into trouble with great energy.

Chapters follow Bones among the Houssa soldiers, a lost tribe, a fetish stick, a frontier code, and a green crocodile. Sanders quietly sorts out what his officers cannot. Wallace's tales mix adventure, humour, and imperial attitudes of their day. They remain lively reading for fans of early twentieth-century colonial adventure.
25266-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
The Reverend Arthur Dimock's Cathedral Church of Saint Paul, published by George Bell and Sons in 1900, describes the old and new buildings of London's great cathedral, with a short historical sketch. Thirty-nine illustrations accompany a text built on manuscripts that grow fuller as the centuries advance.

Dimock recounts preaching that served power, such as Dr. Ralph Shaw's sermon of May 1483 arguing Richard's claim to the throne while Richard listened. He also explains clergy, services, and the bishop's role as visitor. The volume belongs to Bell's popular series for visitors and students of English cathedrals.
26076-birds-from-coahuila-mexico:
Emil K. Urban reports the birds found in Coahuila, Mexico, in a 1959 University of Kansas Museum of Natural History paper. Each account names the birds seen or collected, gives the place and date of the record, and cites earlier reports by other workers. Specimen numbers, wing and tail measures, and notes on plumage help fix which form of each bird was present.

The records range across the state, from sites near Saltillo and Monclova to San Juan de Sabinas, and they draw on field work done in the early 1950s. Urban weighs old claims against his own specimens, at times shifting a bird to a different race when its size or head color fits that form better. The result is a plain state list built on checked specimens rather than on sight claims alone.
26361-the-new-testament-of-our-lord-and-:
This volume gives the New Testament in the common English version as corrected by the final committee of the American Bible Union. This second revision was issued in New York and London in 1866. The revisers worked from the received Greek text, critically edited, and changed the older English only where exact sense or current usage seemed to require it.

The text is set in paragraph form rather than broken by verses, though verse numbers are kept for ease of reference. Quotations from the Old Testament are marked, and passages poetic in the original are set as poetry. The Gospels, Acts, Epistles, and Revelation follow in order, from Matthew's genealogy of Jesus through the closing books.
27022-a-new-subspecies-of-the-black-myot:
E. Raymond Hall and Ticul Alvarez describe a new subspecies of bat in this short 1961 paper from the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History. Until 1928, records of the black myotis, Myotis nigricans, stopped at Chiapas and Campeche in the south.

New Kansas museum collections from eastern Mexico, reaching as far north as Tamaulipas, proved to belong to an unnamed form, which the authors name Myotis nigricans dalquesti. They separate it by size and by small dental marks, such as a broader hypocone and a prominent protostyle, giving mammal students a precise new name for the northern bats.
27079-jonah-and-co:
Dornford Yates's Jonah and Co., first published in September 1922 and many times reprinted, opens with its narrator at Elm Tree Road, a cab ride from St. James's Street. Soon he will prove the journey for the last time, and better men will pace the garden with its high walls, lilies, and laburnums.

The comedy that follows gathers Jonah, Berry, Jill, and Daphne on terraces and in two-seaters, with interchangeable caps bringing luck and Adèle learning the points of a motor. Yates writes light, witty English comedy, where friends, cars, and small confusions carry the day.
27630-a-princess-in-calico:
Edith Ferguson Black published this story with the Union Press of Philadelphia in 1904. Its heroine is seventeen, living at Hickory Farm, where no account is kept of anniversaries.

She stands at her bedroom window before taking up the burden of a new day. Her father is too busy and careworn to remember her birthday, and her mother has gone away. Her stepmother, the second Mrs. Harding, stops for no instant in her ponderous toil, certainly not on washing day. Chapters follow, from Sleepy Hollow and A Ten-Dollar Bill to Pauline's Birthright, Giving Oneself, and Pure Gold.
28214-notes-and-queries-number-236-may-6:
Notes and Queries, number 236, for Saturday, May 6, 1854, is a weekly medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, priced at fourpence. Its notes treat an encyclopaedia of ventilation, the House of Russell, the Duke of Parma, and royal letters to the Grand Masters of Malta. Minor notes cover whipping, salutations, and the Emperor of Russia.

Queries ask for verses, plants, quotations, and facts on Keats, Cowper, and old families, with replies on Addison, Longfellow, and Captain Cook. The number shows Victorian scholars pooling knowledge in print, question by question. It remains a useful snapshot of mid-century antiquarian talk.
28311-notes-and-queries-number-82-may-24:
Notes and Queries, number 82, for Saturday, May 24, 1851, is a weekly medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, priced at threepence. Its notes treat a passage in Measure for Measure, a rhyming Latin song on Robin Goodfellow, Devonshire folk lore on storms, heath-hounds, and Cranmere Pool, and Dibdin's Library Companion. Minor notes cover dress, marriage omens, and a ventriloquist hoax.

Queries ask about vegetable sympathy, court dress, double names, and writers in the North Briton, with replies on villenage and Maclean. The number shows Victorian scholars pooling lore in print. It offers a snapshot of antiquarian talk in the spring of 1851.
28729-travels-in-china-containing-descri:
John Barrow's Travels in China, published by Cadell and Davies of London in 1804 with engravings, reports a short residence at the imperial palace of Yuen-min-yuen. Barrow, late private secretary to the Earl of Macartney and a member of his embassy to the Emperor of China, then journeyed from Pekin to Canton. He dedicates the volume to Macartney and attempts to rank the empire among civilized nations.

Opening chapters correct mistaken notions of the British embassy by the Dutch embassy's reception, and answer a French missionary's account of failure. The Yellow Sea, the Pei-ho or White River, Chinese vessels and navigation, and comparisons with sixteenth-century Europe follow. Readers get an embassy man's China, observant, argumentative, and richly illustrated.
29318-notes-and-queries-number-81-may-17:
Notes and Queries published this number, number 81, on Saturday, May 17, 1851, priced at threepence. The journal called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, genealogists, and others, with the motto, when found, make a note of it, from Captain Cuttle.

This number's notes include illustrations of Chaucer, number six, and Dutch folk-lore. Its queries open with Hepworth Dixon's question on the Blake family, followed by minor queries on John Holywood the mathematician, the irony of Sophocles, the meaning of mosaic, and David Rizzio's signature. Readers get a single week of Victorian scholarly conversation, where small questions and learned answers shared one page.
3006-stalky-co:
Rudyard Kipling wrote Stalky and Co. as school stories about three boys at a bleak English college by the sea. The opening verses praise famous men of little showing, whose work continues greater than their knowing, and recall twelve bleak houses by the shore, seven summers, and two hundred brothers. Masters beat the boys with rods, faithfully and daily, for the love they bore them.

Stalky, M'Turk, and Beetle repay their masters with pranks, impersonations, and cunning, including a letter forged line for line and letter for letter in a housemaster's voice. The book's humor depends on boy slang and school loyalty. It remains Kipling's most affectionate portrait of boyhood, drawn from his own schooldays at Westward Ho.
30106-the-vast-abyss-the-story-of-tom-bl:
George Manville Fenn wrote The Vast Abyss, the story of Tom Blount, his uncles, and his cousins. The file opens with a note calling it one of the very best books by Fenn, with a good steady pace. Yet one keeps wondering how some dreadful situation can be escaped. Young Tom's father, a doctor, died in a recent epidemic that also carried off his mother. Tom was taken into an uncle's house and law business, where he fares poorly.

A different uncle comes visiting and brings Tom home with him to a pleasanter, more interesting life. Together they turn an old windmill into an astronomical observatory, grinding its glass lenses and mirrors and raising the building to standard.
30217-pleistocene-bats-from-san-josecito:
Pleistocene bats from San Josecito Cave are the subject of a Kansas paper signed J. Knox Jones Jr., in volume 9, number 14, pages 389 to 396, dated December 19, 1958. Mammals from the cave near Aramberri in Nuevo León, Mexico, came from field parties of the California Institute of Technology under the late Professor Chester Stock. Earlier workers had reported several groups. During 1950, Professor Stock sent San Josecito material, a portion only, to the University of Kansas for specialists to identify.

That loan held eighty-nine crania and jaw parts of bats, covering three families, Phyllostomidae, Desmodontidae, and Vespertilionidae, and five genera, each with a single species. One species in the set is described as new, while three kinds were then known only from the Pleistocene record. The short paper suits readers of fossil mammals who want cave bats named, counted, and placed with care.
30998-a-new-bat-genus-pipistrellus-from-:
Rollin H. Baker wrote this paper on a new bat of the genus Pipistrellus from northeastern Mexico. It was published in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume 7, number 10, pages 583 to 586, on November 15, 1954. The eastern pipistrelle, Pipistrellus subflavus, occurs in the western part of its range along the Rio Grande and its tributaries, as far west as northern Coahuila and Val Verde County, Texas.

Material collected at those sites belongs to a subspecies never described before, here given the name Pipistrellus subflavus clarus. The type is a female adult, skin and skull, number 48270, taken two miles west of Jiménez at 850 feet in Coahuila on June 19, 1952, by Baker himself. Its known range is northern Coahuila and adjacent parts of southwestern Texas. Its diagnosis notes large size and pale upper parts, near cinnamon-buff.
31084-neotropical-bats-from-western-me-x:
Sydney Anderson's 1960 paper reports new records of tropical fruit-eating bats from western Mexico, published as volume 14, number 1 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. Fruit bats of the genus Artibeus reach their northern limits on Mexico's low coasts, and recent work had split the Mexican species into small and large groups.

Anderson adds specimens of the hairy Artibeus from Sonora, Sinaloa, and Chihuahua, and of two other species from Sinaloa, pushing their known ranges northward. His notes cover variation, distribution, and reproduction. Specimens of Sturnira and Chiroderma from Chihuahua extend those ranges northwestward as well, making the short paper a useful range update for bat workers.
31128-facing-death-or-the-hero-of-the-va:
G. A. Henty's tale of the coal mines, published by Blackie in London and Scribner's in New York, is set in a dreary Staffordshire mining village of brick rows and slate roofs. Thirty-one chapters follow its young hero from evil tidings and a bulldog friend through work in the Vaughan pit and the old shaft. They go on through friendship, a great strike, hard times, an attack on the engine-house, and a great riot.

Later chapters bring a night school, a sewing class, a knotty question, an explosion at the Vaughan, imprisoned miners, a critical moment, and rescue, ending with the hero risen to manager. With eight illustrations by Gordon Browne, the book mixes pit adventure with Henty's gospel of pluck, schooling, and steady character.
31147-a-new-bat-myotis-from-mexico:
E. Raymond Hall's 1962 paper names a new bat, Myotis elegans, from a single specimen taken in northern Veracruz, Mexico. The holotype, an adult female, was collected twelve and a half miles north of Tihuatlán at 300 feet elevation in September 1961 by Percy L. Clifton, and it remains known only from that locality.

Hall describes a small-footed bat with a short tail and small skull, brown upper fur turning golden below, pale brown ears, and a slender, deeply notched tragus. Closest among named kinds to Myotis californicus and Myotis subulatus, it differs in tail, ear, color, and skull form, and the short paper is the formal record of the species.
31149-a-new-pin-on-mouse-peromyscus-true:
Robert B. Finley Jr.'s 1952 paper names a new piñon mouse subspecies, Peromyscus truei erasmus, from lava rocks northeast of Durango, Mexico. Fourteen mice collected there by J. R. Alcorn ran much darker than the piñon mice of adjoining Durango and Zacatecas. Despite a likeness to a form 450 miles to the southeast, their measurements and isolation marked them as distinct.

The type, a young adult female taken eight miles northeast of Durango at 6,200 feet in August 1949, anchors the description. Finley thanks the Kansas University Endowment Association for funding Alcorn's Mexican field work, and the paper remains the source for this dark, lava-dwelling mouse.
31448-mammals-from-tamaulipas-mexico:
Rollin H. Baker's Mammals from Tamaulipas, Mexico, was published as University of Kansas Publications in Museum of Natural History, volume five, number twelve, pages 207 to 218, on December 15, 1951. It reports the mammals of the Mexican state of Tamaulipas. Baker, writing for the University of Kansas, Lawrence, lists species found in the region, with localities and notes on their distribution. The paper was printed at Topeka by the state printer.

Short faunal papers of this kind are the building blocks of mammalogy. Each record adds a dot to a species' map and helps later workers see patterns of range and habitat. For readers of natural history, Baker's paper offers a precise snapshot of Tamaulipas wildlife in the mid-twentieth century, useful to specialists and to anyone tracing the region's fauna.
31683-noteworthy-mammals-from-sinaloa-me:
J. Knox Jones, Jr., Ticul Alvarez, and M. Raymond Lee report, in this University of Kansas Museum of Natural History paper of May 1962, on mammals collected in the Mexican state of Sinaloa. Field parties from the museum had worked there over several of the past twelve years, and this paper sorts what they found.

Its pages give measurements, localities, and notes for the noteworthy kinds, adding to knowledge of a region whose mammals were still unevenly known. Readers get a concise faunal report, written for mammalogists, that turns field collecting into a usable record of Sinaloa's mammal life.
31830-genera-of-leptodactylid-frogs-in-m:
John D. Lynch's 1968 paper for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History revises the genera of leptodactylid frogs in Mexico. In Mexico and northern Central America, about 55 species of eleutherodactyline frogs are known, in the groups Eleutherodactylus, Syrrhophus, and Tomodactylus.

Lynch recognizes four genera on the basis of inguinal glands, the shape of hands and feet, and certain bone features, illustrated by figures such as Tomodactylus angustidigitorum and its lumbo-inguinal gland. Readers get a concise taxonomic revision for herpetologists, sorting a confusing group of small frogs by characters a field worker can check.
32140-a-new-snake-of-the-genus-geophis-f:
John M. Legler's paper, published by the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History on January 28, 1959, describes a new snake of the genus Geophis from Chihuahua, Mexico. It appeared as volume 11, number 4, pages 327 to 334, with two figures. Legler wrote from the University of Kansas at Lawrence, reporting a find from a museum field party.

In July 1957, the party, directed by Sydney Anderson, spent twelve days collecting vertebrates near Creel in southwestern Chihuahua. Among its specimens were two snakes of an undescribed Geophis species. Legler prepared a description and illustrations of the two specimens for publication in spring 1958. Readers get a short, technical species description, grounded in field collection and museum specimens.
32192-peace-with-mexico:
Albert Gallatin's Peace with Mexico, published in New York by Bartlett and Welford at Astor House, is a pamphlet on the terms of peace after war with Mexico. Its first section treats the law of nations, and its argument starts from a stark comparison. Mexico, Gallatin writes, will in the end have to accept whatever peace terms the United States imposes.

Gallatin portrays Mexico as a mixed population of seven million, with very limited resources and no credit. It is torn by feuds at home and by grasping leaders, swinging in turn between lawless rule and rule by soldiers who seized power. Against it he sets a united nation of twenty million, energetic and well supplied, with unlimited resources and credit. Readers get a hard-headed, contemporary case for a dictated peace, grounded in law and in power.
32248-the-standard-cantatas-their-storie:
George P. Upton's The Standard Cantatas, their stories, their music, and their composers, is a handbook published in Chicago by A. C. McClurg and Company in 1888. It is the third volume of a reference series. Upton, author of The Standard Operas, The Standard Oratorios, and Woman in Music, follows the same method as his predecessors. He presents short sketches of the music and stories of the cantatas together with biographies of their composers.

Some biographies are reprinted from the other volumes with small changes, repeated for uniformity's sake, the preface explains. A broad survey of the cantata in all its forms opens the sketches. It runs from a plain recitative or aria style to its present elaborate form. Readers get a Victorian concert-goer's handbook, where each cantata's story, music, and composer are set out in brief, readable sketches.
32495-notes-and-queries-number-80-may-10:
Notes and Queries, number eighty, dated Saturday, May 10, 1851, served as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Priced threepence, with a stamped edition at fourpence, it opens with the Great Exhibition, Notes and Queries itself, and Chaucer's prophetic view of the Crystal Palace. Notes follow on The Lay of the Last Minstrel and poems found among Sir Kenelm Digby's papers.

Folk-lore entries cover the Christmas thorn, milk-maids, disease cured by sheep, and sacramental wine, while minor notes treat luncheon, charades, painters' anachronisms, Spenser's Faerie Queene, and Mary Queen of Scots' prayer. Queries ask about Scandinavia, the rotation of the earth, Irish brigades, and descendants of William ap Jevan. The issue is a lively snapshot of Victorian scholarly chat.
32817-a-new-tortoise-genus-gopherus-from:
John M. Legler names a new tortoise from north-central Mexico in this University of Kansas Museum paper, volume eleven, number five, published April 24, 1959. The new species is Gopherus flavomarginatus, found in taxonomic studies of the genus Gopherus.

The holotype, an adult in the United States National Museum, came from thirty to forty miles from Lerdo, Durango, collected by Dr. Elswood Chaffee in 1918. Legler diagnoses a large tortoise with a flat-topped, posteriorly flared shell, pale laminae with dark centers, and a wider skull than other Mexican members of the genus. Its range lies on the Mexican plateau, where country people call it Tortuga del Monte.
3314-the-city-that-was-a-requiem-of-old-:
Will Irwin writes a requiem for the San Francisco destroyed in 1906. The book recasts a newspaper article of the same title, published in The Sun on 21 April 1906, three days after the visitation came upon the city. It appears here by special permission of The Sun, and Irwin credits Franklin Matthews for the title itself.

An epigraph from Willie Britt sets the tone: he would rather be a busted lamp post on Battery Street, San Francisco, than the Waldorf-Astoria. The old city Irwin mourns is the gay, rough, generous town before the quake and fire. The book is short, elegiac, and firsthand: a newspaperman's farewell to streets he walked and would never walk again.
33410-a-birding-on-a-bronco:
Florence A. Merriam's Birding on a Bronco, published in 1896, tells of bird study on horseback in the American West. Merriam, author of Birds Through an Opera-Glass, opens with Shakespeare's invitation to go a-birding together, and her book follows Mountain Billy under a gnatcatcher's oak and other western scenes. Her illustrations bring birds and bronco to life.

The book's charm lies in its blend of natural history and travel, as Merriam rides, watches, and notes birds with a keen, friendly eye. Its tone is lively and learned, suited to bird lovers and western readers alike. For fans of early nature writing, it is a delightful, pioneering work by a woman who made birding an adventure.
33543-the-amphibians-and-reptiles-of-mic:
William E. Duellman's Amphibians and Reptiles of Michoacán, México, published in December 1961, surveys a rich Mexican state. Its frogs, toads, lizards, and snakes are the subject. Issued as volume fifteen, number one of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History publications, from pages 1 to 148, the paper maps species across Michoacán's varied lands. It has six plates and eleven figures.

The paper suits readers of herpetology, offering a thorough, technical census of a region's cold-blooded fauna. Its tone is precise and systematic, aimed at researchers and students. For biologists of Mexico, it is a landmark source, still cited for what lived in Michoacán before great habitat change.
33778-the-patriot-piccolo-mondo-antico:
Antonio Fogazzaro's Italian novel appeared in English in 1906 as The Patriot, translated by M. Prichard-Agnetti. Its Italian title means a small old world, and the story is set among lake towns and old families in northern Italy. A young man's love, a family feud, and the call of Italian unity pull against each other through three parts.

Scenes of fishing, music, letters, and secret plans build a picture of a society on the edge of change. The hero must choose between home, faith, and country, and the cost of each choice grows clearer as the tale goes on. It remains a rich portrait of Italy before unification was complete.
33898-the-haunted-sentry-box-of-porto-ri:
Lewis Miller wrote this short ghost tale, published in New York in 1916. Below the old fort of San Cristobal at San Juan, a sentry box juts out above the sea at a corner of the wall. Years ago a sentry on that lonely post vanished, leaving only his musket and side-arms, and his loss was blamed on sea-devils.

The same night a beloved priest also vanished, and only his small gold cross, found before the sentry box door, gave a clue. Miller retells the story as he heard it from a man who claimed to know. The tale is a brief, eerie piece of Porto Rican lore.
34121-calavar-or-the-knight-of-the-conqu:
Robert Montgomery Bird's romance Calavar, first entered in 1834 and here in its third edition of 1854, takes up the Spanish conquest of Mexico. Bird calls it the most romantic chapter in the history of the New World, and writes to draw American eyes to that land.

The tale follows the knight of the conquest through Mexico at the time of the Spanish landing, mixing history with high romance. Bird's preface owns both aims at once: to tell a stirring story, and to set a neglected corner of the continent before his readers. Bird's third edition reprints the tale thirteen years after its first appearance, with a fresh preface.
3749-widger-s-quotations-from-project-gu:
David Widger compiled this quote book from the Confessions of Jean Jacques Rousseau, lifting lines that stand alone as maxims. The entries catch Rousseau's frank self study in brief, with remorse that sleeps in prosperity and wakes in storms. A guilty conscience would revenge the innocent, and pride hides incapacity by showing it. Readers can dip in anywhere, since each line carries its own sting or sigh.

The collection serves those who know the Confessions and want to test whether a favorite passage made the cut, since Widger invites additions. It also serves newcomers as a sampler of Rousseau's voice, vain, tender, and quarrelsome by turns. The book is short, and it works best as a bedside browser rather than a substitute for the long confession itself.
42582-a-little-girl-in-old-san-francisco:
A Little Girl in Old San Francisco is a book for the young by Amanda M. Douglas. It came out in New York in 1905 from Dodd, Mead and Company. It is one of a series of Little Girl books, each set in an old American city. A Little Girl in Old New York stands first in the list, with Hannah Ann as its sequel.

A Little Girl in Old Boston, in Old Philadelphia, and in Old Washington stand in the list as well. Old New Orleans, Old Detroit, Old St. Louis, and Old Chicago stand there too, and Old Quebec closes the row. The book at hand is the San Francisco volume of that set, given to Martha Reding, as the dedication page begins. The series brings the past of each city to child readers through a young girl's eyes.
453-emma-mcchesney-and-co:
Edna Ferber follows Emma McChesney, a traveling saleswoman turned partner, in this set of business tales. Emma, now Mrs. McChesney of the Buck Featherloom Petticoat Company, juggles her partner T. A. Buck, her son Jock's letters, and orders from Broadway to Buenos Aires. Each story tests her wit in trade and in life.

Ferber writes with brisk humor and a keen eye for office politics, fashion, and pluck. Emma wins by hard sense, fair dealing, and a sharp tongue when needed. The book charms as a portrait of a working woman who holds her own in a man's trade, and does it with style.
4643-vignettes-of-san-francisco:
Almira Bailey gathers short city sketches in Vignettes of San Francisco, opening with pilgrims going to Rome as a figure. Her vignettes run from the ferry and the Union-street car, through the Latin meeting the Oriental and the pepper and salt man. They go on to the bay on a Sunday morning, Port of Missing Men, Market-street scintillations, cafeterias, and the open board of trade. Police, a marine view, Fillmore Street, and the lobby of the St. Francis follow.

Later sketches meet the garbage-man's little girl, the Palace, and Zoe's garden. They go on to children on the sidewalk, Portsmouth Square, the Fairmont, Van Ness Avenue, fog, a Greek grocer, Golden Gate Park, and the nob of Nob Hill. Bailey writes with warmth about a city of hills, ferries, and mixed peoples. Readers get a charming portrait of old San Francisco, best dipped into sketch by sketch.
5246-modern-french-philosophy-a-study-of:
J. Alexander Gunn's Modern French Philosophy, first published in 1922 with a foreword by Henri Bergson, studies French thought since Auguste Comte. Chapters trace the main currents since 1851, then turn to science, freedom, progress, ethics, and religion, with a comparative table to help readers follow schools and thinkers.

Gunn, a lecturer in psychology at Liverpool, wrote for English readers who wanted a map of a rich philosophical tradition. The book offers a clear survey of French philosophy from the Revolution's aftermath to Bergson's day, and it remains useful as an introduction to thinkers often known only by name.
6076-the-legends-of-san-francisco:
George W. Caldwell celebrates San Francisco on her seven hills, smiling beside an opalescent sunset sea. Bracing air, tingling sea breeze, and rolling fog drive heat languors out and thrill loyal subjects with joy of living. When summer heat oppresses the valleys, the city on the bay stays cool.

Caldwell promises the Indian's reasons for the city's charms and lures, never told before, in legends of hills, fog, and redwood bowers. Winter rains and sun lay a multicolored carpet of flowers on the land. The book gathers local legend into verse and prose, honoring a city of fog, hills, and restless energy.
6205-when-valmond-came-to-pontiac-the-st:
Parker's complete When Valmond Came to Pontiac repeats the introduction of a book standing by itself, an historical fantasy following The Trail of the Sword and preceding The Seats of the Mighty. Appearing in summer 1895, it won gratifying critics, one journal calling it written at a sitting, another a tour de force.

The grave Athenaeum praised it in a key that might make Parker nervous, setting a hard standard to preserve. In truth, Parker says, the book was written, printed, revised, and ready for press in five weeks, its manuscript complete within four. This complete edition is described from its introduction, gathering the lost Napoleon tale.
9364-life-in-mexico:
Frances Calderon de la Barca, born in Edinburgh in 1804, wrote this account of two years in Mexico. Daughter of William Inglis, she married the Spanish diplomat Don Angel Calderon de la Barca and followed his posts to Mexico, Washington, and Madrid. Alfonso the Twelfth later made her Marquesa, and she died in 1882.

With a preface by W. H. Prescott, her letters describe Mexican society, politics, and daily life with wit and keen eyes. She stands between worlds, Scots, Spanish, and Mexican at once. The book remains a classic of travel writing, vivid and humane.
a-counter-blaste-to-tobacco: King James the First blasts tobacco in this famous tract, first printed in 1604. Addressing his countrymen, he argues that even a healthy body is subject to disease, and tobacco adds harm rather than health. Edmund Goldsmid edited this later reprint for private circulation. The Counter-Blaste remains a landmark of early anti tobacco writing.
an-elegy-wrote-in-a-country-church-yard-: Thomas Gray writes his elegy in a country churchyard, presented here with the Eton College manuscript and a note on the texts. The poem meditates on humble lives, death, and unmarked graves, in verses that became among the best known in English. This edition lets readers compare the printed poem with its manuscript form.
animal-sanctuaries-in-labrador-an-addres: William Wood, lieutenant-colonel, presents an address on animal sanctuaries in Labrador before the second annual meeting of the Commission of Conservation at Quebec in January 1911. Printed in Ottawa, the address argues for protecting Labrador's wildlife in reserves. Wood's plea marks an early Canadian step toward conservation. His case still reads as plain common sense.
at-war-with-pontiac-or-the-totem-of-the-:
Kirk Munroe wrote this frontier tale for Charles Scribner's Sons, copyrighted in 1895 and reprinted in 1922 with pictures by J. Finnemore. Munroe sets his story in Pontiac's War, when Ottawa chief Pontiac rose against the British after the French and Indian War. Young Donald and Major Hester carry the action between forts, camps, and wilderness trails.

Chapters promise escapes of prisoners, a baby lost and recovered, and Donald sent on a perilous mission. Pontiac declares war, the major is taken prisoner, and a white medicine man and the totem of the bear shape later turns. Canoe pursuits across a lake, with pursuers yelling once discovered, show Munroe's pace: history delivered as breathless boys' adventure in the Redcoat-and-Redskin manner.
berry-and-co:
Dornford Yates published this set of linked comic tales with Ward, Lock, introducing Berry Pleydell and his circle in book form. A prefatory letter to Valerie confesses the author's dangerous affection for passages in the book. Berry, his wife Daphne, and the faithful Jonah and Boy move between London and the country house White Ladies, where the whole party summers in state.

Domestic logistics supply the war. The household faces leaving town in a month, wholly at the mercy of whoever controls the kitchen at White Ladies. With no restaurants or clubs to fall back on, a bad cook means an unpalatable season. Yates writes upper-class farce in mandarin prose: motor cars, stolen marches, and misunderstandings, all polished until the silliness gleams like good silver.
biographical-memorials-of-james-oglethor:
Thaddeus Mason Harris published these memorials of James Oglethorpe in 1841, dedicating the work to the Georgia Historical Society. Harris, a Massachusetts clergyman and antiquary, honours the founder of the colony of Georgia with a full life. Oglethorpe's example, the dedication verse promises, will shine as a favourite theme with poet and divine, and posterity shall add new honours to his name.

Campaigning in the Georgia backcountry fills the sampled pages. Oglethorpe's party forced through tangled thickets and deep, broken ravines, crossed swamps where horses mired and plunged, and rafted great rivers while the horses swam. Their resolute leader slept in the open air wrapped in his cloak, a portmanteau for his pillow. Harris writes the philanthropic general — prison reformer, coloniser, and soldier — for a young state learning to revere its founder.
britannica-1911-acapulco:
Acapulco is a city and port of the state of Guerrero on Mexico's Pacific coast, south-west of Mexico City, with about five thousand people at the 1900 census. Its deep, semicircular bay is almost land-locked, easy to enter, and so secure that vessels can lie alongside the rocks. The entry calls it the best harbour on Mexico's Pacific coast and a port of call between Panama and San Francisco.

Mountains crowd the town onto a narrow strip of low land and make its climate exceptionally hot and unhealthy. For centuries Acapulco was Mexico's chief Pacific port and the depot for Spanish fleets trading with the East Indies, a trade lost at independence. Hides, cedar, and fruit head its exports.
britannica-1911-alberti-domenico:
Domenico Alberti (about 1710–1740), an Italian player and composer, left his name on a pattern every piano pupil meets: the Alberti bass. He wrote dozens of sonatas on one plan. The tune rides on top from first bar to last, while the bass hand breaks chords into arpeggio runs beneath it. The device grew so common that players tagged it with his name.

His sonatas also mark a shift in taste. The feel for polyphony, the weaving of free voices each with its own line, had worn thin even in Bach's own days, and Alberti's work shows the loss. The pieces hold no other marked traits, the verdict runs. Yet they reached ahead in time. Mozart's first violin sonatas, penned at the age of seven, were most likely built on Alberti's model, though the boy's work outshone it in cleverness.
britannica-1911-alfani-domenico:
Friendship with Raphael shaped the art of Domenico Alfani, a painter born at Perugia near the end of the fifteenth century. Both men trained under Perugino, and they stayed close. Raphael's mark on Alfani's pictures runs so deep that buyers and critics have often handed those pictures to Raphael himself.

Late in life Alfani drifted from his Perugian training toward the newer Florentine manner. Even his death stays unsettled: one account gives 1540, while another has him living in 1553. His works hang at Florence and in a number of churches in Perugia, the city of his birth.
britannica-1911-arauco:
Arauco is a coast province of southern Chile. Concepción bounds it on the north. Bio-bio, Malleco, and Cautin surround it otherwise. Its area is 2,458 square miles. Population was estimated at 70,635 in 1902. The province covered independent Araucania once. That Indian territory was later divided. Four provinces emerged from the division. Arauco was one of them.

Agriculture dominates the province's pursuits. Lebú is its capital town. Lebú stands on the coast. Concepción lies fifty-five miles north of it. A railway connects the two towns. Lebú's population was 3,178 in 1902. The entry is a brief gazetteer notice. It complements the Araucania article directly. Together they map Chile's southern frontier provinces.
britannica-1911-bartolozzi-francesco:
Francesco Bartolozzi (1725–1815), an Italian engraver born at Florence, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. His father was a gold- and silver-smith, and the son was at first meant for that trade. Skill in drawing changed the plan. Florentine artists taught him painting for three years before he went to Venice to study engraving. There he advanced fast and produced work of real importance while still young.

London became Bartolozzi's base for nearly forty years from 1764. There he turned out an enormous number of engravings, many after Cipriani and Angelica Kauffmann, and contributed plates to Boydell's Shakespeare Gallery. His Clytie after Annibale Caracci and Virgin and Child after Carlo Dolce are picked out as his best. In 1802 he moved to Lisbon as director of the National Academy and stayed in Portugal until his death. His son Gaetano was also an engraver.
britannica-1911-berni-francesco:
Francesco Berni (1497–1536) was an Italian poet born at Lamporecchio, near the upper Arno. His family was well descended but very poor. He went to Florence, then to Rome at nineteen. There he served as secretary to Ghiberti, datary to Clement VII. The desk work irked him greatly. Yet Rome made him famous for wit.

The 1911 Britannica entry places Berni at the head of Italian burlesque poets. Mocking comic verse is still called poesie bernesca after him. About 1530 he gained a canonry at Florence cathedral. He died there in 1536, by tradition poisoned by Duke Alessandro. His reworking of Boiardo's Orlando, the Rifacimento, appeared after his death in 1541.
britannica-1911-botzaris-marco:
Marco Botzaris (about 1788–1823) was a Suliot leader in the Greek war of independence, still sung in Greek ballads. Born at Suli in Albania, second son of Kitzo Botzaris, he fled to the Ionian Islands when Ali Pasha took Suli in 1803. There he served in an Albanian regiment in French pay.

He joined the secret patriotic society, the Hetairia Philike, in 1814, and in 1820 made common cause with Ali of Iannina against the Ottomans. When revolt broke he won fame as a partisan leader in western Greece and stood out in the first defence of Missolonghi in 1822–1823. On the night of 21 August 1823 he led 350 Suliots against 4000 Albanians at Karpenisi and routed them, but fell in the fight. His brother Kosta finished the victory.
britannica-1911-bronco: Bronco is a Spanish word meaning rough or rude, applied to an unbroken or untamed horse, in the United States especially a mustang. The whole hosted entry is that single-sentence definition. It gives the word's Spanish root and sense, fixes its American use for a wild or half-wild horse, notes that the word entered America by way of Mexico. The entry warns that the spelling Broncho, though common, is incorrect.
britannica-1911-caracciolo-francesco:
Francesco Caracciolo (1732–1799) was a Neapolitan admiral and revolutionist. He was a prince of a noble Naples family. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his tragic story. He was born on 18 January 1732. He entered the navy young and learned seamanship under Rodney. He fought with distinction in British service. His wars included the American War of Independence. He also fought Barbary pirates and the French at Toulon.

The Bourbon court trusted Caracciolo above all Neapolitans. In December 1798 the king and queen fled Naples. They fled to Sicily on Nelson's ship Vanguard. Caracciolo escorted them on the frigate Sannita. Even his loyalty was shaken by the king's cowardly flight. At Palermo he asked leave to return to Naples. The city was drunk on French revolutionary ideas. The aristocracy and middle classes welcomed him with enthusiasm. He was pressed to join the new republic or flee.
britannica-1911-cariaco:
Cariaco is a town on the north coast of Venezuela. It is also called San Felipe de Austria. It stands 40 miles east of the city of Cumaná. It sits at the head of the gulf of the same name. Its population was estimated at 7000 in 1908. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives its trade. The town stands a short way up the Cariaco river.

Its port, right on the coast, is called Puerto Sucre. The district around Cariaco grows several cash crops. Cotton, tobacco and cacao are its named products. Cattle and fruit also come from the district. Trade through Puerto Sucre is considerable, the entry says. Yet that port has no regular link with foreign ports. The whole notice is a brief paragraph in the original. It gives the site, the port and the farm produce.
britannica-1911-cavalli-francesco:
Francesco Cavalli (1599?–1676) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian composer born at Crema. His real name was Pier Francesco Caletti-Bruni. Cavalli was the name of his patron, a Venetian nobleman. He became a singer at St Mark's in Venice in 1617. He rose to second organist in 1639, first organist in 1665, and maestro di cappella in 1668.

His fame, though, rests on his operas. He began writing for the stage in 1639. Paris summoned him in 1660 to produce Serse at the Louvre for the marriage of Louis XIV. He returned in 1662 with Ercole Amante. Twenty seven of his operas survive, most of them at St Mark's library in Venice. The entry credits him with making opera a popular entertainment. He trimmed Monteverde's large orchestra, added tuneful arias, and used popular types in his libretti.
britannica-1911-crispi-francesco:
Francesco Crispi (1819–1901) was an Italian statesman born at Ribera in Sicily on 4 October 1819. He set up as an advocate at Naples in 1846. When revolution broke out at Palermo in January 1848 he hurried home and helped guide the rising. The Bourbon return in 1849 shut him out of the amnesty and drove him to Piedmont. There he lived poorly by journalism and plotted with Mazzini's circle.

Crispi helped organize Garibaldi's expedition of the Thousand in 1860 and drafted the proclamation at Salemi. He entered parliament in 1861 for Castelvetrano on the extreme Left. The later pages trace his rise to power and his firm foreign policy. He courted good relations with France yet refused to bend to pressure or dictation. Criticism of him, the entry says, fixed more on his private life and his circle than on his public acts.
britannica-1911-fontana-domenico:
Domenico Fontana (1543-1607), Italian architect and mechanician, was born at Mili, a village on Lake Como, in 1543. After good training in mathematics he went in 1563 to join his elder brother, who was studying architecture at Rome. He advanced fast and entered the service of Cardinal Montalto. For him he built a chapel in Santa Maria Maggiore and the villa Negroni. When the pope stopped the cardinal's pension, Fontana offered to finish the works in hand at his own cost.

The cardinal was soon elected pope as Sixtus V, and he made Fontana his chief architect at once. The Lateran palace, the Quirinal palace and the Vatican library are among his works. His highest fame came from moving the great Egyptian obelisk that Caligula had brought to Rome. The entry tells how the huge stone was raised and set up, the engineering feat by which Fontana is still remembered.
britannica-1911-geminiani-francesco:
Francesco Geminiani (c. 1680–1762) was an Italian violinist, born at Lucca about 1680. He took music lessons from Alessandro Scarlatti. He studied the violin under Lunati, called Gobbo, and then under Corelli. In 1714 he came to London, where the earl of Essex took him under his care. He made his living there by teaching and by writing music. In 1715 he played his violin concertos with Handel at the English court.

After a stay in Paris, Geminiani came back to England in 1755. In 1761 he went to Dublin, where a servant stole a music draft on which he had spent much time and work. His grief at that loss is said to have hastened his death in 1762. The article calls him a first-rate player, but finds most of his works dry and short on tune.
britannica-1911-guardi-francesco:
Francesco Guardi (1712–1793) was a Venetian painter. He was a pupil of Canaletto. He followed his master's style very closely. His pictures are often attributed to Canaletto himself. Yet the difference, once seen, is marked. Canaletto is firmer, solider and more distinct. Guardi shows a more spirited touch. His colour sparkles, and his figures are sketched with flair.

Guardi sometimes coloured Canaletto's own designs. His speed was extraordinary. Three or four days could produce an entire work. That facility, and a love of gain, made his output large. Many of his works are found in England. Seven hang in the Louvre. The entry is a compact judgement on a painter long standing in his master's shadow.
britannica-1911-guicciardini-francesco:
Francesco Guicciardini (1483–1540) was an Italian historian and statesman. He was born at Florence in 1483. His family had held Florence's highest posts for generations. Marsilio Ficino held him at his baptism. He studied at Ferrara and Padua until 1505. An uncle's death tempted him toward the church. His father forbade any son entering so corrupt a body.

Guicciardini turned instead to law. At twenty-three he lectured publicly on the Institutes. He married Maria Salviati for political support. He says so frankly in his own memoirs. In 1512 Florence sent him as ambassador to Ferdinand of Spain. His Spanish letters show extraordinary powers of observation. Critics accused him of betraying Florence for the Medici. A long career as diplomat and governor followed. His great history of Italy crowns the later account.
by-right-of-conquest-or-with-cortez-in-m:
G. A. Henty wrote a boys' tale of the fall of Mexico, with twenty-two chapters and a preface. The preface sets the wonder plain. A vast realm, full of warlike folk, fell to a mere handful of Spaniards. No tale maker would dare such a plot, Henty holds. Brave men and better arms tell part of it.

A stark offer and a start for unknown parts open the run. Voyage, isles, and wreck lead to Anahuac. A fine land, Tezcuco, and life in a palace fill the first ashore part. Cortez steps in at the eleventh chapter. Flight, the Cholula killings, and entry to Mexico mark the heart. Treasure room, revolt, and the causeway fight fill the late run. A victim for the gods and a road home close the list. One lad's eyes carry the great clash for young readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-de-maris:
Adam de Marisco, or Adam Marsh, was a Franciscan probably from Somerset, whose birth date is unknown. He died at the end of 1257 or start of 1258. Educated at Oxford, where he won a great reputation, he had served three years as Wearmouth's rector in Durham before joining the Friars Minor about 1237. At the Oxford Franciscan house he succeeded Robert Grosseteste as lecturer.

His correspondence shows how wide his personal influence ran. It illustrates the moral force of the early Franciscans in England. Intimate with Grosseteste, Archbishop Boniface, Richard of Cornwall, and Simon de Montfort, he helped give Earl Simon his deep interest in reform. He died just as the great crisis of Henry III's reign began. Roger Bacon called him and Grosseteste the greatest clerks in the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-steu:
Agostino Steuco, Steuchus, was an exegete born at Gubbio, Umbria, in 1496. He died at Venice in 1549. At seventeen he joined the Lateran Canons Regular at Gubbio. In 1525 he became director of Cardinal Grimani's library at Venice; in 1530, prior of Reggio's canons. Early in 1538 Paul III appointed him Bishop of Kisamos in Crete.

Paul III also put him over the Vatican Library on 27 October of the same year, though in that post he did not accomplish much. In 1547 Paul III made him legate to the Tridentine Council, transferred to Bologna; he died returning to Rome. A man of varied talents, he knew history, philosophy, and theology well, with Greek and Hebrew. His chiefly exegetical works appeared in three volumes from Ambrogio Morando, Paris 1578 and Venice 1591 and 1601.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-amico: Antonio Amico, a canon of Palermo who died in 1641, wrote church history for Syracuse and Messina. His works also covered Sicily's kings and admirals. The same short entry adds Bernardino, a Neapolitan Franciscan who died in 1590. As prior at Jerusalem he wrote a 1609 treatise on the plans and images of the holy buildings there, illustrated by Callot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-and-leo:
Carlo Marenco was an Italian dramatist born at Cassolo in Piedmont in 1800 who died at Savona in 1846. After studying law he chose literature, supporting himself with a Treasury post at Savona. A Romantic, he rejected the unity of time and gave his plots fuller development than classic rules allowed. His figures feel alive and his diction is polished, though his tragedies lean toward the sentimental.

Dante inspired several of his tragedies, including Pia de' Tolomei, Corso Donati, and Conte Ugolino, beside historical plays such as Arnoldo da Brescia and Corradino. His son Leopoldo, born at Ceva in 1831 and dead in 1899, followed him into the Treasury and then into drama, teaching Latin literature from 1860. Leopoldo's many plays, from Celeste and Saffo to Piccarda Donati, also draw on Dante and on modern and medieval history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuzco:
A diocesan entry sketches Cuzco, a suffragan see of Lima in Peru. The city, capital of its department, lies 11,000 feet above sea level on the eastern end of the Knot of Cuzco. The original Inca city, reputedly founded in the eleventh century and destroyed by Pizarro in 1535. Remains of the Inca palace, the Temple of the Sun, and the Temple of the Virgins of the Sun survive.

Among the finest later buildings stands Santo Domingo cathedral. The diocese, erected by Paul III in 1536, covers Cuzco and Apurimac. It spans 21,677 square miles, with a Catholic population of 480,000. It counted 106 parishes, 650 churches and chapels, 150 priests, a seminary, and schools at the time of writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durango-mexic:
Durango in Mexico is an archdiocese in the northwest of the country. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry dates its founding to 28 September 1620. Seventy-two years earlier, friars Diego de la Cadena and Geronimo de Mendoza had founded a mission in the Sierra Madre valley, San Juan Bautista de Analco. Captain Ibarra of Spain founded the city itself in 1554, and missionaries made it their hub at once.

Their work among the natives bore such fruit that under Philip the Third, Guadalajara was split by Paul the Fifth and Durango rose to episcopal rank. Its first bishop, Gonzalo Hernandez y Hermosillo, gave much time to the Indians' welfare. At first the diocese held New Mexico, Chihuahua, and Sonora, later made sees of their own. The city, also called Guadiana, stands at sixty-seven hundred feet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-el-greco:
El Greco was one of the most striking Spanish painters, born in Crete between 1545 and 1550 and dead at Toledo in 1614. In 1570 the miniaturist Giulio Clovio wrote to Cardinal Farnese praising him as a Cretan then at Rome who had studied under Titian. Yet El Greco took little from Titian, and his work stands apart, with only traces of Bassano, Baroccio, Veronese, and Tintoretto.

He reached Spain in 1577, signed his name in Greek letters, and always called himself a Cretan. At Toledo in 1582 he spoke before the Inquisition as interpreter for a countryman accused of being a Moor, and there he settled for good. Famed for cold blue tones, greys, and many whites, he painted in a manner that looked ahead by a century and a half. His greatest work is the Burial of the Count of Orgaz in the church of Santo Tome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filippo-brune:
Filippo Brunellesco was a Florentine architect and sculptor born in 1377 and dead in 1446. Trained first as a goldsmith, he turned to sculpture and then gave himself wholly to architecture. He was among the chief leaders of the early Renaissance in architecture. He first applied the rules of perspective to art in a set, reasoned form.

His crowning work was the dome of Florence cathedral, which he raised without centering. The dome used pointed octagonal arches and a double shell, with stairs and passages between them. A lantern crowned the dome and added sixteen metres to its height of ninety-one metres. He also built the sacristy dome of San Lorenzo and the charming freestanding Pazzi Chapel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fra-angelico:
Fra Angelico, born Guido di Pietro near Vicchio in Tuscany in 1387 and dead at Rome in 1455, was a Dominican friar. He was one of the most beloved painters of the Florentine school. He joined the Dominicans at Fiesole in 1407 with his brother Benedetto. He began as an illuminator of missals and choir books, and grew into a painter of religious scenes marked by simple naturalness and deep piety.

His best-known work is the fresco cycle in the convent of San Marco in Florence, alongside Madonnas, a Coronation of the Virgin, and an Adoration of the Magi. Frescoes on the lives of St. Lawrence and St. Stephen fill the Chapel of St. Nicholas in the Vatican. His technique was slender by later standards, but the entry presents his gentle, prayerful art as the reason his name endures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-ami:
Francesco Amico, born at Cosenza on 2 April 1578, was one of the great theologians of his age and a Jesuit of profound humility. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1596, taught theology for twenty-four years at Naples, Aquila, and Gratz, and spent five years as chancellor of the academy at Gratz. His method was scholastic, shaped to fit a four-year course of teaching, and his doctrine is described as following St. Thomas, brief, clear, subtle, and solid.

His works cover God one and three, the nature of angels, the last end, faith, hope, and charity, and justice and right, besides the Incarnation and the sacraments. One treatise, on justice and right, was banned in 1651 until corrected, because of three propositions objected to by Popes Alexander VII and Innocent XI. A corrected edition of 1649 was allowed. The entry ranks him among the foremost Jesuit theologians of the seventeenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francescoe-de:
Francesco de Vico, born at Macerata on 19 May 1805 and dead at London on 15 November 1848. He was a Jesuit astronomer who gave the Roman College observatory a European reputation. Entering the Society of Jesus at Sant' Andrea in Rome, he showed a gift for mathematics and astronomy and became professor of those subjects. He assisted director Father Dumouchel, and succeeded him as director in 1839.

He won the French Academy's Lalande prizes and six times took the King of Denmark's gold medal for the first discovery of a telescopic comet. One medal now rests in the museum at Georgetown University. Driven from Rome by the political disturbances of 1848, he was invited by Arago to stay in Paris. He chose Georgetown College's new observatory instead, reaching America on 22 July 1848. He died at London that November, on his way, still at work for the science he loved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Franco, often called Il Semolei, was an Italian historical painter and etcher born at Udine in 1510, who died at Venice in 1580. He studied at Rome with close attention to Michelangelo, favoring large allegorical decorations. A Catholic Encyclopedia article remembers him less for painting than for his etchings, of which more than a hundred survive.

He worked with Vasari on decorations for Ottaviano de' Medici, and painted portraits of the Medici family, largely copies from other men. His designs for majolica for the Duke of Urbino mattered in their day. His plates, signed B.F.V.F., run somewhat mechanical in execution, yet carry a light, easy spirit. About half are original, while the rest follow Raphael, Titian, and others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-lanf:
Giovanni Lanfranco, also known as Cavaliere Giovanni di Stefano, was a decorative painter born at Parma in 1581, who died at Rome in 1647. As a boy page at Piacenza he showed a talent for drawing and was placed under Agostino Carracci. Before sixteen he had painted a Virgin and Saints admired enough for Sant' Agostino at Piacenza. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a bold rival of Domenichino.

After Carracci's death he assisted Annibale Carracci in the Farnese Gallery and Roman churches. By scheming he won a commission promised to Domenichino. In the cupola of Sant' Andrea della Valle he painted his greatest work, the Virgin seated in clouds, grand and daring in design and coloring. At Naples he finished Domenichino's treasury cupola, destroying most of his rival's work, and Urban VIII later knighted him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huanuco:
Huánuco is a suffragan diocese of Lima in Peru. Its department covers over fourteen thousand square miles with a population of about one hundred and forty-five thousand in 1896. The capital, also called San León de Huánuco, stands on the upper Huallaga, a tributary of the Amazon, nearly six thousand feet above sea level, with about seven thousand five hundred people.

Huánuco ranks among Peru's oldest Spanish colonies, founded in 1539 by Gómez de Alvarado at Pizarro's instance, four years after Lima. Indians levelled the first houses in revolt, and after Pizarro's murder a new colony entered the valley.
